10.1002_adfm.79332: P2‐type Fe/Mn‐based layered oxide materials have long been plagued by structural degradation, air sensitivity, and interfacial instability, which severely restrict their application in sodium‐ion batteries. Herein, we propose an in situ modification strategy integrating bulk Li/F co‐doping with a surface heterojunction coating and successfully synthesize Na 0.67 Fe 0.35 Mn 0.5 Li 0.15 O 1.93 F 0.07 (LMO@NFMLOF). IDPC‐STEM reveals the heterogeneous structure comprising distinct inner and outer regions. DFT calculations confirm the presence of a built‐in electric field at the heterointerface. The experimental results demonstrate that bulk Li/F co‐doping enhances crystal stability, while the built‐in electric field generated by the surface heterojunction accelerates Na + kinetic processes, and the coating further improves air and interfacial stability. Consequently, the LMO@NFMLOF cathode delivers a discharge capacity of 110 mAh g − 1 after 200 cycles at 2C. Remarkably, it maintains a discharge capacity of 85.6 mAh g − 1 after 300 cycles at 5C, demonstrating outstanding rate capability and cycling stability. This synergistic bulk‐surface optimization provides a new approach for designing high‐rate layered oxide cathodes.
10.1016_j.ces.2026.124276: The rapid growth of lithium-ion battery (LIB) applications necessitates recycling technologies that are efficient, economically viable, and environmentally sustainable. A key challenge is optimizing black mass (BM), the mixture of cathode and anode components produced during pre-treatment. This study evaluates how variations in black-mass composition along the pre-treatment route, defined as Black Mass 1 to 4 (BM1-BM4), influence thermal behavior, reaction pathways, and economic potential during pyrometallurgical processing, with the aim of identifying the most suitable feedstock. Thermodynamic simulations were conducted using FactSage 8.2 to investigate equilibrium phase assemblage over 100–2000 °C, while economic assessment was performed for materials processed at 600 °C. The results show that BM1 and BM2 generate complex solid and liquid products dominated by multi-component metallic solid solutions and intermetallics, which hinder downstream separation. In contrast, BM3 and BM4 form simpler phases that are readily compatible with hydrometallurgical purification. Gaseous phase behavior also differs significantly: BM1 releases both flammable and toxic gases, BM2 and BM3 primarily generate toxic emissions, whereas BM4 emits only oxygen, representing the safest option. Energy-demand analysis indicates that BM1 and BM2 exhibit predominantly exothermic behavior with minimal external heating requirements, while BM3 and BM4 are fully endothermic and require continuous heat input. Economically, BM1 shows the highest laboratory-grade value due to the formation of specialty compounds, whereas BM3 and BM4 perform best at the industrial grade, supported by abundant market-stable metals and oxides. Overall, BM3, and particularly BM4, emerge as the most promising feedstocks for large-scale pyrometallurgical recycling followed by hydrometallurgical refining.
10.1016_j.uclim.2026.102787: Floods are among the most frequent natural disasters globally and increasingly are exacerbated by climate change and urbanisation. With the evolution of flood management practices over the past decades, the concept of resilience has also gained prominence as a valuable component of the decision-making toolbox. The resilience concept emphasizes the need to supplement conventional engineering solutions with improvement and adaptation measures that mitigate individuals and communities at risk. Nevertheless, a gap remains in the comprehensive understanding of how community communication can facilitate the improvement in flood resilience, particularly in the Global South. This study examines how flood risk communication (FRC) affects individual protection actions to enhance resilience at the community level. Specifically, behavioural theories are integrated with Protection Motivation Theory to form a conceptual framework to provide details of the processes that influence individuals' threat and coping appraisals. As a case study, a dataset consisting of 297 online survey responses from residents living in 10 flood-prone municipalities across Thailand was collected and structural equation modelling was employed to analyse the data. The findings suggest that effective FRC should include risk assessment, stakeholder responsibilities, and preparation measures, and the sharing of such information was positively associated with higher levels of threat and coping appraisals. Moreover, accessibility and trustworthiness of information were found to play a critical role in increasing coping appraisals. Overall, this study highlights the importance of understanding how FRC can affect individual preparation intentions and enhance flood resilience. • Resilience has become a key aspect of flood management, supplementing traditional engineering solutions. • Effective flood risk communication (FRC) can enhance community resilience but is not well understood, especially in the Global South. • This study uses Protection Motivation Theory (PMT) as a theoretical basis to analyse individual protection actions. • A survey of 297 residents from 10 flood-prone municipalities in Thailand was conducted, using Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) to assess the impact of FRC on threat and coping appraisals. • Key elements of effective FRC include: risk information, stakeholder responsibilities, and preparation measures, accessibility and trustworthiness of information; and is found to be crucial in enhancing individual preparation intentions.
